method: code-only; no rig actuation; consolidations must keep existing tests passing unchanged

findings.status: FIXED — but incompletely at first; see F8
findings.summary: interactive CLI on/off/cycle ignored the operation lock, so `off` during a dump cut VBUS
findings.detail: _busy_guard consulted active_op_on_slot, which reads only the charge/drain/workbench task registries. A dump, wanze run or flash holds the OPLOCK, which lives in the config file precisely so a separate process can read it. So an interactive `asteroid-docking-bay off <watch>` would cut power under a running 4 GB transfer — the exact failure the lock was introduced to prevent.
findings.not_the_gap: The systemd charge timer was already covered from the other side: _web_busy_slots reads `held` from /api/status (#41). But that only works while the web service is up; the lock in the config is readable regardless, so reading it directly is the stronger check and the only one an interactive command has.
findings.fix: _busy_guard now checks oplock.held(load_config(), serial) first, mirroring rpcops._refuse_if_busy. Purely additive — it can only refuse, never actuate.
findings.test: test_cli_power_commands_refuse_a_watch_held_under_an_oplock; written failing first, and it also pins that an EXPIRED lock does not block.

findings.summary: JS fetch call sites are too varied to collapse behind a helper
findings.detail: 78 fetch statements; only 13 are near-uniform, and those split into two sub-shapes of 6-7 one-liners each (POST->refresh, POST->toastRes). A generic jfetch() would save a handful of characters per site and obscure the ones that differ. Recorded so the next audit does not re-measure it.

findings.summary: Escape did not close the msgs or guide panels; the show/hide convention was written out eight times
findings.detail: Every floating panel is <div id=X> plus <div id=Xmask>, and showing/hiding one is the same three lines. That was repeated across four open and four close functions. The cost was not the repetition itself but that each new panel had to remember to join every list by hand — which is how the Escape handler ended up closing only `reg` and `bt`, the two panels that existed when it was written.
findings.fix: panelShow/panelHide own the mask convention; panelHideAll finds panels by CLASS rather than by a list, so a panel added tomorrow is covered without touching the handler.
findings.line_delta: +6 code lines (+13 with comments) — this consolidation does NOT save lines. It replaces eight copies of a convention with one definition and removes a class of bug.
findings.test: test_escape_closes_every_panel_not_just_the_first_two; plants both the hardcoded-list regression and a panelHide that forgets the mask.

findings.summary: _run defaults to timeout=None, so the status path's device listing could hang a thread forever
findings.detail: util._run(cmd, check=True, timeout=None) waits indefinitely unless a caller passes a timeout, and 18 call sites do not. The one that matters most is adb_devices_checked -> `adb devices -l`, which runs on every status build: a hung adb server would block that thread for ever rather than failing.
findings.fix: adb_devices_checked now passes a deliberately generous 20s bound — far longer than any healthy or degraded call, so it can only fire where the alternative was hanging. Safe because the failure was ALREADY handled correctly: rc != 0 reads as 'call failed' (None), not 'no devices', and _wait_adb_state discards failed samples rather than treating them as watches that vanished.
findings.test: test_the_device_listing_cannot_hang_forever — pins both the bound and the failed-vs-empty distinction.

findings.summary: `fastboot devices` is implemented twice, and only one of the two is bounded
findings.detail: _fastboot_devices() (fastboot.py:23) runs `fastboot devices` with NO timeout. _fb_list_refresh (fastboot.py:81) runs the same command with timeout=8 and a docstring warning that the scan takes 5-8s and 'ignores the subprocess timeout'. Two implementations of one listing, with different hang behaviour and different parsing.
findings.why_not_fixed: _fastboot_devices feeds _wait_for_fastboot, which is on the FLASH path. Changing its timing under stress is exactly what this audit refuses to do unattended. It is also the more interesting half: the two should become one function, and that is a shape decision, not a mechanical edit.
findings.suggested: One lister with an explicit bound, used by both the warmer and the flash wait; keep the cache in the caller, not in the lister.

findings.summary: every oplock holder releases on every path
findings.detail: Three holders: watch.dump (worker releases in a finally; an explicit release if the thread never starts, with the reasoning in a comment), oplock.set (user-driven), wanze.probing_set (user-driven). The 4h expiry covers the remaining hairline between hold and thread start. No leak found.

findings.summary: the wearability verdict is still protected by a sample/duration floor
findings.detail: An in-progress drain_rate can be noisy early (a 2-minute reading yields ~30%/h) and is shown live, which is honest. But it cannot become a watch's canonical est_h: _latest_drain_summaries enforces _DRAIN_MIN_SAMPLES and _DRAIN_MIN_HOURS, citing audit B4. Verified the earlier fix is real and still in place.

findings.summary: drain elapsed time is wall-clock, so a clock step corrupts a run
findings.detail: elapsed_h = (time.time() - task['start_ts'])/3600. A NTP step or manual clock set during a multi-hour run skews the rate. Recorded rather than 'fixed' because wall clock is the DEFENSIBLE choice here: the task is persisted and resumable across a service restart, and a monotonic clock does not survive that. A real fix would record both clocks, or sanity-bound elapsed_h, and is a design decision for mo.

findings.summary: slow status refreshes are load-dependent, not chronic
findings.detail: Only 2 refreshes over 1s in a 40-minute window with most of the fleet shelved; earlier in the evening, with many watches live, it logged continuously at 1.1-2.2s. The breakdown attributes it to the 'render' phase (the per-port loop). Not chased: optimising without the load present is guesswork. If it is worth pursuing, sub-instrument the render loop first so the next slow refresh names the culprit rather than the phase.

findings.summary: 20 of 36 modules were missing from docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, which still said 0.4
findings.detail: The map a new contributor reads first had drifted badly between 0.5 and 1.0. Undocumented modules included rpcops (the op table the container split treats as its security boundary), rpc, oplock (the cross-process lock), orbit, registry, stockrom, wanze and icecc.
findings.why_it_matters: Not pedantry: the map is where someone looks to find out whether the thing they need already exists. An incomplete map is a direct cause of the duplication this audit was asked to hunt.
findings.fix: All 36 modules described, in their own docstrings' words; header moved to 1.0; the dependency section now covers rpc/rpcops and names the one acknowledged cycle (webstatus -> rpcops via a local import).
findings.test: test_every_module_is_in_the_architecture_map — fails if a module is absent, so the document cannot silently drift again. That absence of a test is why it drifted.

findings.summary: a docstring claims to mirror logic it does not mirror
findings.detail: webstatus._ssh_battery says it 'Mirrors rpcops._reachable_transport's selection'. It does not: _reachable_transport falls back to an ORBIT member's WiFi address, and _ssh_battery has only the ssh_reach_ip branch.
findings.assessment: The CODE is right — orbit members get battery from last_seen via the warmer, so a docked-SSH read has no business probing orbit. The COMMENT is the defect, and a dangerous one: someone 'aligning the mirror' would add a network probe per SSH watch per status refresh, which is exactly the 4.25s render regression _detect_rndis was written to remove.
findings.suggested: Reword to say it mirrors only the assigned-SSH-address branch, and why the orbit branch is deliberately absent.

findings.summary: two callers reach past Dispatcher.dispatch into the private _data dict
findings.detail: cli.cmd_status and webstatus.finish_ssh_relocation call DISPATCH._data['op'](args) directly. Dispatcher.dispatch(op, args) exists and raises RpcError for an unknown op; the private path raises KeyError instead, so a renamed op becomes a traceback rather than a clean error.
findings.suggested: Use dispatch() in both. Small and safe, but it belongs with the webstatus->rpcops cycle it is entangled with, which is a shape decision for mo.

findings.summary: the interactive `charge` command had NO claim check at all
findings.detail: F1 guarded on/off/cycle and I assumed the remaining uhubctl_set_power sites were legitimately owned by their own operations. Classifying all seven showed that was wrong: cmd_charge -> _charge_one powers a port on and off with neither the oplock nor the task store consulted.
findings.impact: Two failures. During a dump it cuts the transfer. During a DRAIN TEST it powers the port mid-run, recharging the watch while the test keeps sampling — which does not fail loudly, it invents a result. That is verbatim the scenario _busy_guard's own docstring says destroyed five hours of readings.
findings.not_the_gap: The systemd timer (cmd_check_charge) is a separate entry point, guarded from the other side by _web_busy_slots. Deliberately unchanged.
findings.lesson: F1 shipped as 'fixed' on an unverified assumption about the other call sites. Finishing a shipped fix outranks finding a new one.
findings.test: test_interactive_charge_respects_a_busy_or_locked_port — covers both an oplock and a drain owning the slot. Uses a tripwire on the first call past the guard: asserting only 'no power switched' let the planted bug run the real charge loop and HANG the suite instead of failing.

findings.summary: USB descriptor strings reached the DOM unescaped, and a serial went raw into a click handler
findings.detail: Two seams. (1) The guided setup builds its read-back text from product, serial and path straight off the bus (watch_devices_on_bus) and interpolated it into innerHTML RAW — so a device whose USB product string contains markup could run script in the UI. Guided setup is exactly the flow where unknown hardware is plugged in one piece at a time. (2) mkstrip's Battery-Info handler put the serial into a single-quoted JS string inside an HTML attribute unescaped, while the codename beside it was escaped; three sibling openBI sites already used jsq().
findings.standard: This project already treats a device-supplied serial as untrusted in a SHELL (the dump command quotes it). The DOM gets the same treatment now.
findings.census: 51 interpolations of device-supplied fields: 47 already escaped, 2 URL-encoded, 2 raw — both fixed.
findings.testing_note: The first version of the serial assertion was VACUOUS — it ran in a harness where the handler was never rendered, so both assertions passed on absent text. Splitting it into a minimal harness exposed that. A second plant then also passed because it patched one of four openBI sites rather than the one under test.

findings.summary: restore_plan encodes the beluga procedure as if it were universal, and cannot express nemo's proven one
findings.detail: Two restores are proven and they are structurally different. beluga (2026-08-03): flash system, vendor, cache, recovery, boot from the dump plus the FACTORY EMPTY userdata.img. nemo: moWerk's canon FAILED, and what worked was system + boot + userdata + metadata + keystore + cache, ALL from that same watch's own dump, then fastboot continue (misc is untouchable there — its bootloader refuses both erase and flash).
findings.the_problem: restore_plan(parts, names) raises on anything that is not classified 'firmware'. It therefore refuses userdata, metadata (unknown) and keystore (safe_erase) — so nemo's PROVEN procedure cannot be built by the code at all.
findings.the_insight: The safety rule is not 'never restore userdata or per-device state'. It is 'never restore state from a DIFFERENT unit'. nemo's working restore used its own coherent dump, which is safe; the same partitions from another watch would not be. Provenance is the gate, not partition class — and fingerprint_gate already exists to establish provenance.
findings.why_not_fixed: Relaxing a hard safety stop is not a night edit. It also needs mo's whitelist: procedures assigned per watch/family, only TESTED ones enabled, sibling inference (all LGs, all ASUS) marked as inference rather than evidence. beluga is an outlier; the newer layouts (sol/aurora, GKI A/B with a dynamic super partition) are untested for restore entirely.
findings.suggested: A PROCEDURES table keyed by codename: partition list, userdata source (factory-empty | own-dump), evidence (tested date+serial | inferred from sibling), default REFUSE. restore_plan takes the procedure rather than assuming one.

findings.summary: mooneye's restore procedure recovered from the porting transcripts — a THIRD distinct method
findings.evidence: meta-smartwatch session 82e99b58, 2026-07-06T16:38-16:46, mooneye M6600TB1Z300 (Mobvoi, Wear OS 8.0 Oreo).
findings.sequence: fastboot flash boot <own stock boot> ; fastboot erase userdata ; fastboot erase cache ; fastboot reboot -> booted to stock Wear OS ('tap to begin').
findings.system_not_flashed: The sparse system flash FAILED (remote: 'Unknown chunk type') and turned out to be unnecessary: '/system was pristine stock, and we never needed the sparse flash'. So the proven mooneye path does not write system at all.
device_constraints: mooneye's MediaTek lk bootloader rejects img2simg sparse output — it groks only RAW/DONT_CARE, not FILL. Any future system write needs a FILL-FREE sparse image.
No separate vendor partition: /vendor is a symlink into /system.
/data is FBE-encrypted with keys in the TEE, which is why ERASING userdata is correct and restoring a foreign userdata would not be.
findings.caveat: The boot flashed in that session was a MODIFIED stock boot (ro.debuggable / adb_keys baked) for the Bluetooth investigation. A pure restore should flash the stock boot from the watch's own dump. The method is proven; that one substitution was not part of the goal.
findings.so_there_are_three: beluga (5 partitions + factory EMPTY userdata), nemo (system+boot+userdata+metadata+keystore+cache, all from its own dump), mooneye (boot + erase userdata + erase cache). Three genuinely different procedures across three vendors — which is exactly why the whitelist has to be per watch, not derived.

findings.summary: mo's 'old layout + no keystore -> simple method' hypothesis is machine-checkable, and both tested watches fall on the predicted side
findings.method: Streamed the first 32 KB out of every archived dump (7z/tar.gz/tar.zst) and parsed the GPT with stockrom.parse_gpt. Read-only, no rig, no full extraction — a 7.65 GB archive costs a few seconds this way.
findings.validation: mooneye: 18 partitions, NO keystore — and the simple method (boot + erase userdata + erase cache) is PROVEN on it. beluga: 40 partitions, HAS keystore — and it is the one that needed the intrusive factory-empty-userdata recipe. Two tested cases, both on the predicted side.
findings.caution_family_lines_do_not_hold: The split does NOT follow vendor families cleanly: wren and sparrow are 29 partitions with no keystore, while swift is 43 WITH one. So 'all the ASUS behave the same' is not supported by the layouts — the whitelist should key on the watch (and ideally on a layout check of its own dump), not on an assumed family.
findings.limits: n=2 on the tested side, so this is support, not proof. 'No keystore' is a proxy for mo's 'old layout'. nemo's archive yielded no GPT in the first 32 KB (its tar member is probably not the raw image), so nemo is absent from the table.
findings.suggested: a-d-b can gate on this automatically: parse the dump's GPT and refuse the simple procedure on any layout carrying keystore / A-B slots / super. That is a read-only check on a file the user already has.

findings.status: CORRECTION — a-d-b's own dump path is UNTESTED
findings.summary: the sol dump was the PORTING session via an initramfs, not a-d-b's runtime dump op
findings.evidence: Every dump command lives in -home-mo-Git-meta-smartwatch session 82e99b58 on 2026-08-08: `adb -s 0123456789ABCDEF exec-out "dd if=/dev/mmcblk0" > mmcblk0-dump1.img`, the sha256 pair, and a mkmanifest.py that imported a-d-b's stockrom for parse_gpt/classify. The only asteroid-docking-bay hit is this audit's own search command two minutes earlier — self-noise, the exact trap the attribution work documented.
findings.method: The manifest says it plainly: method 'initramfs-clean' — dumped from AsteroidOS's own initramfs booted off a FLASHED init_boot on slot B, with userdata never mounted. So it is not the runtime path at all.
findings.what_is_actually_proven: dd over adb exec-out as a TECHNIQUE, from an initramfs, by the porting session, verified by two full 31.4 GB dumps with matching sha256 and 81/81 partitions identical.
findings.what_is_NOT_proven: a-d-b's own watch.dump op — the UI button — which takes a RUNTIME dump of a booted, rooted AsteroidOS watch. Its only attempt was hoki on 2026-08-15, which died at 85 MB when the hub reset the whole 1-3 cascade.
findings.correction_of_my_own_correction: Earlier in this session I said 'the dump is unproven', mo corrected me with the sol result, and I accepted it too broadly. The method is proven; a-d-b's FEATURE is not. Both statements needed narrowing, and this is the accurate one.
findings.for_1_0: This is exactly the gap mo wants closed: dump a watch through a-d-b's own op, on a quiet cascade, and verify it with the new compare-dumps command.

findings.summary: the runtime dump needs a per-watch procedure table too, with at least three methods

methods.steps: unlock the bootloader; on the FIRST boot after unlocking, boot the debug ramdisk using the boot image's kernel; dump immediately from the rooted adb environment of that ramdisk.
methods.why_preferred: Fewest steps, and userdata is never mounted — which is what makes the resulting image trustworthy per partition rather than only for the quiescent ones.

methods.status: mo's description — NOT verified by this session
methods.steps: unlock the bootloader; let Wear OS restore itself and boot again; re-enable adb; push the ext4 to /sdcard/ on the watch; return to the bootloader and `fastboot boot` the boot image.

methods.status: mo's recollection, hedged by him ('afair') — NOT verified
methods.steps: as the temp install, but needs MANUAL intervention to put the device into the boot image's recovery sideloading mode.

findings.consequence: Dump procedure and restore procedure are both per-watch properties, so the whitelist should carry BOTH. Unlocking the bootloader is a precondition for every one of them — which also means a locked watch cannot be dumped at all, matching what watch.fbreport already records per serial (bootloader_unlocked).
open_questions: Do temp-install-sdcard and beluga-temp-install differ ONLY by the manual recovery-sideload step, or in the flashed artefact too?
Which boot image is 'the bootimage' in each method — AsteroidOS's own, or a device-specific one?

findings.summary: dump method is chosen per watch by capability, and the multi-step path needs a stepped guide
findings.rule: Where `fastboot boot` of a debug ramdisk is PROVEN to work, always offer that clean method. Otherwise fall back to the runtime dump, which works on any watch that allows a temp install (what users call dual boot). Initramfs is preferred whenever available.
findings.capability_model: Two per-watch booleans decide the offer, and both are things a watch either does or does not do: ramdisk_boot_works -> clean initramfs dump; temp_install_works -> runtime dump. Neither is derivable from the codename, so both belong in the same whitelist as the restore procedure.
findings.stepped_guide: The runtime dump needs several manual steps with the device changing state between them (unlock, let Wear OS boot, re-enable adb, push the ext4, return to the bootloader, fastboot boot). So it needs a guide that leads step to step with WAITING BREAKS until the device appears in the required state.
findings.the_mechanism_already_exists: That is precisely the guided-setup step machine built 2026-08-15 for onboarding: instruction -> user acts -> 'Check now' -> a hardware read-back gates the advance, never a ticked box. Its read-backs are already the ones this needs — a watch in fastboot, a watch on adb, a watch answering as root. The step machine generalises from 'onboard watches' to 'any procedure with stop points and hardware read-backs', which is a reuse rather than a second implementation.
findings.needed_from_mo: Which watches have PROVEN fastboot-boot-ramdisk support. That is the whitelist input; sol is the one this record can confirm.
